title: Say it in your own words
goal: Three sizes of the same job: say one sentence a new way, say the point of a chunk, say the main idea of the whole text.

card.title: PARAPHRASE · GIST · MAIN IDEA
lines: Paraphrase one sentence: COVER IT → SAY IT → CHECK IT. Same meaning, different words.
Gist of a chunk: WHO OR WHAT? → MOST IMPORTANT THING? → TEN WORDS.
Main idea of the whole text: TOPIC + WHAT THE TEXT SAYS ABOUT IT.
The topic is a few words. The main idea is a full sentence.

copy.label: almost a copy
copy.feedback: That is the same sentence with one or two words changed. Cover it and say it like you are telling a friend.

meaning.label: the meaning changed
meaning.feedback: The words are new, but it does not say the same thing as the text.

first.label: the first sentence
first.feedback: That is the first sentence of the chunk. Is it the most important thing, or just the first thing?

detail.label: a detail
detail.feedback: That is one detail or example. What is the detail there for? Say the bigger thing.

topic.label: only the topic
topic.feedback: That names the topic. It does not say what the text tells you about it.

H.label: half right
H.feedback: Part of it is right, but it goes too far or leaves out half of the text.

levels.description: Meaning kept and most content words changed.
Meaning kept but mostly the same words, or words changed and the meaning drifted.
Copied, or the meaning is lost.
One sentence a stranger who read the chunk would accept as its point.
The first sentence copied, a detail, or an opinion.
A few words that name what the whole text is about.
A detail, a full sentence about one part, or off topic.
One sentence with the topic and what the text says about it.
The point without the topic, or too narrow (covers one part only).
Topic only, a detail, or the student's own opinion.

thrift.title: Second-Hand by Choice
sentences: Thrift stores used to be places people shopped only when money was tight.
That has changed.
Today, many teenagers choose second-hand clothes on purpose, even when they could afford new ones.
Part of the reason is price.
A hoodie that costs sixty dollars new might cost eight dollars used.
But price is not the whole story.
Many teens say they want clothes that nobody else at school has, and a thrift store rack is full of one-of-a-kind items.
There is also a bigger reason.
Making new clothes uses a lot of water and energy, and much of what is made ends up in landfills within a year.
Buying used clothes keeps them out of the garbage for longer.
Thrift shopping takes patience, though.
Sizes are mixed up, some items are stained, and you may leave with nothing.
For the teens who love it, the hunt is part of the fun.

jobs.title: Working While in School
sentences: Many high school students work part-time.
Some work to save for college, some to help their families, and some simply want their own money.
Studies of working teens often show a pattern.
Students who work up to about ten hours a week often do as well in school as students who do not work.
Students who work more than twenty hours a week are more likely to see their marks drop and to miss classes.
The difference seems to be time and energy.
A short shift leaves room for homework and sleep.
A long shift, especially on a school night, does not.
Counsellors suggest that students who need to work keep their hours low during the school year and pick up more in the summer.

esports.title: A Different Kind of School Team
sentences: Two years ago, playing video games at Northfield High could get a student sent to the office.
Now the school has an official esports team.
Its twenty players practise after school and compete online against other schools.
Coach Maria Santos says the team has reached students who never joined anything before.
Several players told her they had not been part of a club or a sport until now.
To stay on the team, players must attend class and keep their marks up, and most of them have.
Not everyone was pleased at first.
Some parents worried that the team would mean even more screen time.
The coach answered by limiting practice to two afternoons a week and adding stretching breaks.
After one season, most of those parents came to watch the final match.
esports.tutorNote: Northfield High and the people in this passage are invented.

sections.title: One sentence, a new way
sections.tutorNote: I DO then WE DO. Teach cover-say-check on one sentence, then two choose-the-best items, then three sentences said aloud before they are typed. Paraphrase is always oral first.

text: To paraphrase is to say one sentence a new way.
A friend who did not read it should learn the same thing from your sentence.
COVER the sentence. SAY it your way. CHECK: same meaning? different words?
Changing one word is not enough. Changing the meaning is not allowed.

reveals.label: Read it
reveals.text: A hoodie that costs sixty dollars new might cost eight dollars used.

reveals.label: Cover it and say it
reveals.text: You could pay eight dollars for a used hoodie instead of sixty for a new one.

reveals.label: Check: same meaning?
reveals.text: Yes. Both say the used one is much cheaper.

reveals.label: Check: different words?
reveals.text: Yes. Most of the words changed. That is a paraphrase.

sections.title: The point of a chunk
sections.tutorNote: I DO on chunk 1, WE DO on chunks 2 to 4, with support fading: chunk 2 is choose-only (who or what, then best gist); for chunks 3 and 4 the student says and types a gist first, then checks it against three options. The player highlights one chunk at a time.

text: After a few sentences, stop and say the most important thing.
Ask two questions. WHO OR WHAT is this chunk mostly about? What is the MOST IMPORTANT THING it says about that?
Then say it in ten words or fewer.
A gist leaves out examples and numbers.

sections.title: Topic and main idea
sections.tutorNote: I DO then WE DO. The four chunk gists from the thrift passage should be on screen or on paper. Main idea is the sentence every gist fits under. Expect the topic to be offered as the main idea; use the frame 'Thrift stores ... what?'

text: The TOPIC is what the text is about. It is a few words.
The MAIN IDEA is what the text says about the topic. It is a full sentence.
Main idea = topic + what the text says about it.
A good main idea is one that every chunk fits under.

reveals.label: Look at the four gists
reveals.text: By choice. Cheap and one-of-a-kind. Better for the environment. Takes patience but fun.

reveals.label: Main idea
reveals.text: Many teens now choose thrift stores because used clothes are cheap, unique and better for the environment, even though it takes patience.

reveals.label: Check
reveals.text: Does every chunk fit under that sentence? Yes. If one did not, the main idea would be too small.
